Selective attention.q: While reading a great book on a noisy bus, you don't notice the conversation next to you. What is this?
wrong: Inattentional blindness to an object right in front of you
That is missing a visible object, not tuning out sound while focusing.
Selective attention.exp: Focusing on one stimulus and not others.

Stroop effect.q: You're asked to say the ink color of the word RED printed in blue, and you hesitate. What is this?
wrong: The cocktail party effect of picking out one voice
That is about focusing on one voice.
That is something different grabbing attention.
Stroop effect.exp: The word fights the color, slowing your reaction.

Change blindness.q: In a video, a person's shirt changes color between shots, and most viewers never notice. What is this?
wrong: Inattentional blindness to an object that is always there
Nothing was missed entirely; a change was missed.
Change blindness.exp: Missing a change because attention is elsewhere.

Inattentional blindness.q: While counting basketball passes, viewers completely miss a person in a gorilla suit walking through. What is this?
wrong: Change blindness, missing that something has changed
Nothing changed; a visible object was missed.
The gorilla did not pop out for them.
That is the weakest detectable stimulus.
Inattentional blindness.exp: Failing to see a visible object when attention is elsewhere.

Change vs. inattentional blindness.q: What is the key difference between change blindness and inattentional blindness?
Change vs. inattentional blindness.right: Missing a change vs. missing an object
wrong: One involves hearing while the other involves vision
Both are about attention to what you see.
Both happen because attention is elsewhere.
Change vs. inattentional blindness.exp: Change blindness = not noticing a change; inattentional blindness = not seeing an object at all.

Cocktail party effect.q: At a loud party, you can follow your friend's voice and tune out everyone else. What is this?
wrong: The Stroop effect, a conflict between word and color
Cocktail party effect.exp: Focusing auditory attention on one voice.

Hearing your name.q: In a noisy cafeteria, you suddenly notice someone across the room say your name. What explains this?
Hearing your name.right: Your brain registers your name in background noise
wrong: Clairvoyance, perceiving events you didn't witness yourself
No scientific basis, and you did hear it.
This is part of the cocktail party effect.
Hearing your name.exp: Part of the cocktail party effect.

Pop-out phenomenon.q: In a crowd of people dressed in black, the one person in bright yellow catches your eye instantly. What is this?
wrong: Selective attention to something you chose to focus on first
You didn't choose it; it grabbed you.
Pop-out is about something different grabbing attention.
Pop-out phenomenon.exp: Something different pops out to get our attention.

Bottom-up processing.q: Your skin registers cold air and sends that signal up to your brain. Which kind of processing is this?
wrong: Top-down processing, using what you already know
That uses knowledge to interpret, not raw input.

Top-down processing.q: You see a blurry shape in your dark bedroom and realize it's your coat, because you know where you hung it. Which processing is this?
wrong: Bottom-up processing, raw input from the senses
Your knowledge is doing the work here.
That is the weakest detectable stimulus.
Top-down processing.exp: Using knowledge and context to interpret: perception.

Reading scrambled words.q: You can read "Tihs sneetnce is esay to raed" without much trouble. What explains this?
wrong: Bottom-up processing of every single letter in order
You read words as wholes, not letter by letter.
Reading scrambled words.exp: The mind reads the word as a whole when first and last letters are right.

The handwriting example.q: In a messy note, you notice squiggles (sensation) and then realize they say "15" (meaning). Which part is top-down?
wrong: Seeing the ink marks on the paper before knowing their meaning
The handwriting example.exp: Awareness of squiggles = bottom-up; knowing what they mean = top-down.

Absolute threshold.q: A hearing test plays a tone more and more softly. The softest level you detect half the time is what?
wrong: Your difference threshold, the change you can notice
That is about noticing a change between two stimuli.
Absolute threshold.exp: The weakest stimulus detected 50% of the time.

Absolute threshold examples.q: Which is one of your slides' examples of an absolute threshold?
Absolute threshold examples.right: Hearing a watch tick 20 feet away
wrong: Noticing music jump from level 5 to level 10 in the car
That is a just noticeable difference.
Seeing a gorilla in a video
Absolute threshold examples.exp: Watch at 20 feet, a teaspoon of salt in two gallons, car music volume.

Difference threshold (just noticeable di.q: Your mom turns the TV volume up one notch and you don't notice, but at three notches you do. What did three notches pass?
wrong: The absolute threshold, the weakest sound you can hear
You could already hear the TV.
Difference threshold (just noticeable di.exp: The minimum change noticed 50% of the time.

JND example.q: Car music is on level 5. According to your slide, which change are you most likely to notice?
wrong: From 5 to 6, just one level louder than before
Too small a change to notice, per the slide.
JND example.exp: 5 to 6 is probably unnoticed; 5 to 10 is noticed.

Weber's law.q: Adding one candle to a room lit by 2 candles is obvious, but adding one to a room with 100 candles isn't. Which law explains this?
wrong: The all-or-none principle of how a neuron fires
Weber's law.exp: Differences must be a constant percentage, not a constant amount.

Weber's law examples.q: Using your slide's 2% rule, how much would you need to add to a 100-ounce weight to notice the difference?
wrong: About 1 ounce, the same as for a 10-ounce weight

Extrasensory perception (ESP).q: A friend claims she can sense things without using her senses. What does science say about this?
Extrasensory perception (ESP).right: There is no scientific basis for ESP
wrong: It has been proven in many careful lab experiments over the years
Psychic visions are no better than guesses.
It is a type of bottom-up processing
Extrasensory perception (ESP).exp: Telepathy, clairvoyance and precognition lack scientific support.

Telepathy.q: A man claims he can send his thoughts straight into his twin's mind. What ESP claim is this?
wrong: Clairvoyance, seeing events you weren't present for
That is mixed senses, and it's real.

Clairvoyance.q: A psychic says she can "see" where a missing person is hidden without having been there. What ESP claim is this?
wrong: Precognition, perceiving events in the future
She is claiming to see a present or past event.
That uses real senses and knowledge.

Precognition.q: A woman claims she dreamed about a plane crash before it happened. What ESP claim is this?
wrong: Telepathy, sending thoughts straight to another mind
That is seeing events you weren't at.

Psychics and the police.q: Police get tips from a psychic about an unsolved case. How useful are they, according to your slides?
Psychics and the police.right: No more accurate than others' guesses
wrong: Usually more accurate than the evidence gathered by detectives
Psychics and the police.exp: Psychic visions are no better than guesses.

Why psychics seem accurate.q: A psychic makes 50 predictions a year and one comes true. Why do people still believe in her?
Why psychics seem accurate.right: They remember hits and forget misses
wrong: Most of her predictions turn out to be completely correct
Why psychics seem accurate.exp: So many predictions guarantee a hit, and people forget the misses.
